title: Wto/99
address: 3519 N Clark St, SUITE C301, Chicago, IL, 60657
description:
Building from a roughly 1,000 hour archive, WTO/99 reanimates the ideological conflicts that drew thousands to the streets of Seattle in hopes for a better future. The film is an immersive visual artifact of a week that brought 40,000 people together to warn of environmental collapse, the vanishing middle class, and what the full inclusion of China in the World Trade Organization would mean for our collective future. The protesters—seen as a rabble-rousing nuisance at the time, yet appearing prophetic today—were met with extreme violence by a militarized police force, an all-too-fitting way to usher in a new century; one that is now defined by US failure to address climate change and increasing state aggression.
This immersive archival documentary depicts the four-day clash between the then-emerging World Trade Organization (WTO) and the 40,000+ people who took to the streets of Seattle in 1999 to protest the WTO Conference and sound the alarm on the WTO’s impact on human rights, labor, and the future effects of continued globalization.

title: Kat Edmonson: Have Your Merry Christmas with Me
description:
This holiday season, acclaimed vocalist Kat Edmonson returns with a dazzling new chapter in her celebrated career: the November 6, 2026 release of her latest album, Have Your Merry Christmas With Me, followed by a nationwide tour beginning Thanksgiving and continuing through the end of December.
Have Your Merry Christmas With Me by Kat Edmonson plays like the soundtrack to a classic romantic comedy—lush, witty, soulful, and filled with longing, flirtation, and holiday warmth. Romantic bossa novas mingle with a tropical, 1960s-cocktail-party take on “Jingle Bells,” the swinging jazz-gospel exuberance of “Hark! The Herald Angels Swing,” and an achingly soulful transformation of Allen Toussaint’s “It’s Raining” into “It’s Snowing.” Two beautifully crafted originals, “Have Your Merry Christmas With Me” and “Hush! There’s a Falling Snow,” feel instantly at home among the standards, with the timelessness of future holiday classics. 
Bringing the music to the stage, Kat Edmonson’s 2026 Have Your Merry Christmas With Me Holiday Tour promises an unforgettable evening of festive charm, featuring sparkling new selections alongside beloved songs from her acclaimed catalog. After enchanting audiences year after year, she returns with the warmth, wit, and effortless elegance that have made her one of today’s most distinctive jazz vocalists. 
Kat is a Songwriters Hall of Fame award-winning singer and songwriter whom The New York Times has described as having “an equal foothold in jazz, cabaret and vintage cosmopolitanism pop.” She has appeared on Austin City Limits, NPR’s Tiny Desk Concerts, A Prairie Home Companion, and The Tonight Show, and has performed at venues and festivals including Carnegie Hall, the Montreux Jazz Festival, and the Blue Note in Japan. Her original songs have appeared in film, television, and advertising. Edmonson also appeared as a 1930s jazz singer in Woody Allen’s Café Society and made her theatrical debut in the Drama Desk Award-nominated off-Broadway production The Hang by Taylor Mac and Matt Ray. As NPR observed, “Hearing Edmonson makes it virtually impossible to do anything but stop and listen.”
Blending nostalgia, celebration, and holiday spirit, this concert feels both classic and new, with all the makings of a cherished seasonal tradition.

title: Created Equal: The Premises and Promises of the Declaration of Independence
location: Regenstein Library, The Special Collections Research Center
description:
On July 2, 1776, the Continental Congress voted to declare independence from Great Britain. Two days later, delegates in Philadelphia finalized a document designed to announce and explain that act to readers in America and Europe.
 The Declaration of Independence asserted the revolutionary right of a people to alter or abolish a government, grounding that principle in the “self-evident” claims that “all Men are created Equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights” and “that among these are Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness.”
 Over time, many readers have come to consider the radical philosophical premises in the Declaration as founding political promises of the United States. In doing so, they transformed an indictment of the British King and a manifesto of secession from the British Empire into an American charter of liberty, equality, and rights.
 But the Declaration’s meaning has never been solitary. From the start, readers disagreed about what its authors intended. Since 1776, radically different interpretations of the Declaration’s ideas have been put to different ends—from demands for the legal, political, and social equality of all persons, to claims for the rights of states to secede from the union, to calls for the revolutionary overthrow of the government.
 How did the Declaration’s premises become its promises? Drawing on rare materials from the seventeenth century to the present, this exhibition invites you to explore the document’s meanings in its own time, to consider contested interpretations across history, and to reflect on what the Declaration means today.
 Curator
 Eric Slauter, Associate Professor, Department of English Language and Literature; Associate faculty member, Divinity School; Founding Director of the Karla Scherer Center for the Study of American Culture; The University of Chicago
 Visitors
 This exhibition is free and open to all. Visitors to the University of Chicago Library may obtain an entry pass by checking in at Regenstein Library’s entry desk and presenting a current, government-issued photo ID, such as a driver’s license, CityKey, state ID, or passport to confirm identity. Get more visitor information.
 Exhibition Gallery Hours: Weekdays, 9 a.m. to 4:45 p.m.

title: Sewn as One
description:
Sewn as One is a textile installation by the Science, Art, and Sustainability (SAS) team of the Phoenix Sustainability Initiative (PSI), in partnership with Creative Chicago Reuse Exchange (CCRx). On view in the 2nd Floor South Cantilever Lounge at the Logan Center for the Arts.
 The Phoenix Sustainability Initiative (PSI) is a student-led organization at the University of Chicago dedicated to promoting environmental awareness and integrating sustainable practices throughout campus and surrounding communities. Through collaborative partnerships, inclusive community-building, and creative approaches to environmental challenges, PSI encourages students to develop the skills and collective agency necessary to enact tangible change. Its Science, Art, and Sustainability
 (SAS) project group brings these commitments into artistic practice, exploring how material reuse, collective making, and creative experimentation can cultivate environmental responsibility and meaningful connections.
 Collaborating with Creative Chicago Reuse Exchange, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that redistributes donated surplus materials for artists, hobbyists, and educators, the SAS project group transforms upcycled fabrics into a tapestry of collective care and environmental awareness. Through a series of open, hands-on mending workshops, the project invites participants to reconsider mark-making not only as gaining technical skill, but as a social and ecological practice.
 Over the course of two academic quarters, three-hour “Sewing Sunday” sessions were held by SAS and open to anyone on campus or passing through the work space, encouraging both experienced makers and first-time participants to sew, patch, embroider, and mend donated textiles. Each contribution—a series of stitching, patchwork, or conversation—becomes part of the evolving textured surface of the work.
 The accumulated labor, dialogue, experimentation, and learning from these sessions culminated into the large-scale fabric installation that spans the hallway of Logan Center for the Arts’ South Cantilever Lounge. The final tapestries act as visual records of foregrounding sustainability, slow making, and community engagement while tracing how individual acts of care can coalesce into an exuberant, communicative form.

title: Time, Fragmented
description:
Time, Fragmented asks what it means for a place to be shaped by complex social and environmental histories, and how distinct but interrelated histories coalesce to create a collective narrative. Along these lines, the exhibition considers contemporary practices of unearthing, both literally and figuratively, and investigates remnants of times past, piecing together the story that unfolds thereafter. In the context of shifting regional powers and migrating stories, Time, Fragmented illuminates the (hi)stories foundational to modern-day Turkey, tracing diasporas of culture, thought, and practice.
 Materials entail historic postcards and photographs from the turn of the twentieth century displayed from a family collection by İbrahim Selim Ergöz. Additionally, building and ornamental materials from the Joel Snyder Materials Collection are displayed alongside photographs and maps from historic expeditions from the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures Archives. Finally, multi-media works from New Orleans-based Turkish artist, Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes are presented alongside personal ephemera from the artist and curator. Through a variety of items from polyphonic sources, Time, Fragmented engages with the many layers of history—witnessed through a mosaic of lived reality, filtered through glimpses of past experiences—that live in time.
 Curator
 Time, Fragmented is curated by Defne Ergöz, BA/MA ’27, an Environment, Geography, and Urbanization major and Architectural Studies minor in the College, concurrently pursuing an MA in Art History.
 Artists
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes (Turkish, b. 1997)
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes lives and works in New Orleans, Louisiana since 2024. Türkoğlu Hewes is a conceptual photographer, building worlds for a single frame that carry the immaterial nature of emotions to a physical realm, portraying their silent dictate on lived experiences. The artist focuses on conflicting collective and personal agendas, evaluating dynamics between discipline and intuition, culture and callings. Her Turkish identity and upbringing rooted in strong familial ties appears in her recent work completed in İstanbul. The coexistence of culture and nature in her work criticizes the misconception of full control over emotional environments, similar to the power assumed over natural ecosystems. Türkoğlu Hewes studied fine arts, film and theater at Northwestern University. Her work has been exhibited in the 2025 Louisiana Contemporary at the Ogden Museum of Southern Art. She has been included in exhibitions at Soho Photo Gallery in New York City, Barın Han in İstanbul, and the Contemporary Art Center in New Orleans.
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz (Turkish, b. 1971)
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz, the curator’s father, currently resides in Westchester, New York. Ergöz has been collecting antique ephemera since he was fifteen, with a vast collection spanning his interests in historical documentation and postal items, especially as it concerns the Middle East North Africa region. His archive ranges from widely-available materials to rare collectibles. Time, Fragmented is the first instance Ergöz’s collection will be on public display.

 CWAC Exhibitions is organized by the Department of Art History’sVisual Resources Center. Additional support for the exhibition is provided by the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, the Committee on Environment, Geography, and Urbanization, the Master of Arts Program in the Humanities, and Architectural Studies.
 The CWAC Exhibitions team includes Katie Chen, Scarlet Ding, Jiayi Laura Feng, Natalie Hsu, Grace Newby, Kseniya Portnaya, Stephanie Strother, and Yanlin Zhu.

title: A Sneak Peek on the Dark Side: First DarkSide-20k Analysis Workshop
location: The University of Chicago John W. Boyer Center in Paris
description:
A wide range of astrophysical and cosmological measurements indicates that the universe is filled with far more matter than what we can account for by looking around us. This excess matter is called dark matter and, while it is thought to be constituted by a new, exotic species of elementary particle, its nature remains unknown — making it one of the biggest puzzles in modern particle physics and cosmology.
 DarkSide-20k (DS-20k) is an experiment currently under construction at the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso, beneath the Apennine Mountains in Italy. It aims to detect the potential feeble interactions of dark matter particles using an innovative detector featuring a 50-tonne target of specially sourced argon, extracted from underground gas reservoirs in Colorado and depleted in the radioactive isotopes that typically contaminate argon extracted from air. This massive, low-background target, instrumented as a two-phase Time Projection Chamber, is expected to feature a sensitivity to dark matter exceeding that of any currently running experiment.
 The event, held at the University of Chicago’s John W. Boyer Center in Paris, is the first collaboration-wide analysis workshop — previous workshops were much smaller in scale — and aims to kickstart the finalization of the study of DS-20k’s sensitivity to dark matter. By the end of the workshop, the organizers aims to be able to run the full simulation and analysis pipeline, evaluating the final sensitivity of the experiment while accounting for the finer details of the detector response. The workshop will also train a new cohort of researchers to become core members of the analysis team in preparation to early data. The event is organized by the International Institute of Research in Paris, with primary support from The University of Chicago and the Université Paris Cité, and with the participation of AstroCeNT.

title: Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive
description:
Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive brings together album covers, book jackets, magazines, film stills, photographs, prints, and other ephemera featuring the work of Charles White (1918-1979) to examine the expansive cultural life of his imagery. Tracing how his work circulated beyond the studio and the museum wall, the exhibition reveals how White’s images centered everyday life and shaped a broader visual language.
 An artist who worked fluidly across drawing, painting, printmaking, and mural-making, White created what he described as “powerful images of dignity”, centering African-American experiences as well as historical figures and events at a time when such representations were widely distorted or excluded from mainstream culture. These opportunities for reproduction arose through active collaboration with musicians, writers, and filmmakers. White’s images were adapted, printed, and distributed across a wide range of media, crossing disciplines and communities to become part of a shared cultural consciousness.
 By foregrounding circulation alongside creation, the exhibition invites visitors to consider how White’s work contributed to the formation of a Black visual canon. His images did not remain fixed objects behind glass — they became living symbols, connecting people, histories, and communities through a sustained commitment to representation, relationships, and what White himself understood as a sense of oneness.
 Charles White Across Media: A Visual Archive is a special initiative of the Charles White Archives presented by Logan Center Exhibitions and the South Side Community Art Center. The exhibition is curated by Ian White with curatorial support by Paulina Alvarez, Jan Brugger, and jada-amina. Additional support is provided by the Ng Family Visiting Artist Fund, the Revada Foundation, and Friends of the Logan Center.

title: Anne Frank The Exhibition
location: Griffin Museum of Science and Industry
address: 5700 S Lake Shore Drive, Chicago, IL, 60637
description:
ANNE FRANK: THE EXHIBITIONat Griffin MSI
Anne Frank The Exhibition is an immersive, full-scale recreation of the Annex where Anne Frank, her family and four other Jewish inhabitants lived in hiding during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands. Griffin Museum of Science and Industry is the first museum in the Midwest to present this exhibition, and Chicago is only the second U.S. city to host this extraordinary experience, featuring never-before-seen artifacts from Anne Frank’s life. 
Explore the world that shaped Anne’s story, from her early childhood in Frankfurt through the rise of Nazi Germany and the spread of antisemitism across Europe, to the Frank family’s move to Amsterdam. There, Anne lived for nearly ten years, including the final two, which were spent in hiding. 
Step inside the meticulously reconstructed Annex and reflect on the daily challenges, risks and courage of those who hid there before their arrest and deportation in 1944.
Anne Frank The Exhibition is a presentation of the Anne Frank House.

title: Neuroscience Seminar Series: Daniel Kronauer, PhD
location: Knapp Center for Biomedical Discovery, Room 1103
description:
Neuroscience Seminar Series
 Tuesday, December 1st, 11:00 am
 Daniel Kronauer, PhD
Rockefeller University
 KCBD 1103
 “Ant Societies: From behavior to neural circuits”
 Abstract: The colonies of social insects are complex biological systems in which manifold interactions between individuals give rise to emergent properties that are adaptive at the group level. However, most social insects cannot be propagated in captivity or genetically manipulated, severely limiting the scope for experimentation. Over the past fifteen years, we have developed and utilized the clonal raider ant, Ooceraea biroi, as a new model species that overcomes many of these limitations, allowing us to study social dynamics and underlying mechanisms under controlled laboratory conditions. Our work has led to a deeper understanding of how ants within a colony assume distinct behavioral roles and efficiently divide labor, how they communicate, both as adults and across different developmental stages, and how these interactions result in collective behavior. Additionally, our research has shed light on how evolution has repurposed and expanded genetic, neural, and physiological mechanisms from solitary ancestors to produce highly social organisms. In this seminar, I will provide an overview of this work and discuss future directions in our research program aimed at understanding the evolution and organization of insect societies, spanning from genes to neural circuits and behavior.
 Host: Annika Sharma, CON (Heckscher Lab),
 Committee on Neurobiology

title: Autumn Carillon Tower Tours
description:
Carillon Tower Tours are at 11:30 AM and 4:30 PM Tuesdays - Fridays.
 The Laura Spelman Rockefeller Memorial Carillon and its sister instrument at Riverside Church in New York City, both dating from the early 1930s, were the masterworks of the Gillett & Johnston bell foundry of Croydon, England. Carillons of this size had never before been made, and have not been made again since that time. The Chicago instrument, comprising 72 bells and 100 tons of bronze, is the single largest musical instrument ever built. Its bells were cast over a three-year period and include a massive 18.5 ton bourdon sounding a low C#.
 In 271 steps we can show you the bells from the perspective of our carillon students and peregrine falcons! The spiral stone staircase is taken at a leisurely pace, and is not recommended for those who are claustrophobic. Along the way you’ll walk above the Chapel’s false ceiling (the attic, via a catwalk), through the mechanical room housing the original carillon regulator clock as well as the pneumatically-driven mechanism of the quarter and hour chimes, past the largest bell (36,926 lbs at 117 inches in diameter) and its 13 friends, and then into the playing cabin, 240 of the 271 steps up, where the carillonneur plays the mighty instrument. Beyond the cabin, another short winding staircase leads the way to the top of the tower. In season and when permitted by the University, magnificent 360-degree views of Chicago, Lake Michigan, northern Indiana, the Michigan Harbor Country shoreline, and the University itself are available.
 Please note that the tour is not suitable for children under the age of 5. Young children and anyone unable to ascend the stone steps may watch the recital free of charge in the Chapel itself from one of two viewing stations in the west transept and narthex. Check in at the front desk to set off for the 45-minute round-trip climb. Carillon tours are capped at 15 guests.
 The carillon is played live in recital each weekday of the academic year at 12 PM and 5 PM, and on Sunday mornings after the 11 AM service. Members of the University of Chicago Guild of Carillonists are happy to incorporate requests into the daily recitals.

title: Guided Tour of the Newberry
description:
In 1893, the World’s Columbian Exposition took place in Chicago, Grover Cleveland started his second non-consecutive term as president, and the Newberry building opened to the public. On this guided tour, you’ll learn about the history behind the founding of the Newberry. You’ll also discover all the ways you can engage with the library today.
Founded in 1887, the Newberry had three temporary locations before moving into its permanent home across from Washington Square Park in 1893.
The library was designed by architect Henry Ives Cobb, with input from Newberry head librarian William Frederick Poole. Cobb envisioned a grand edifice on par with the civic landmarks of Europe; Poole favored a more modest design that would facilitate user access to books and other resources. In the end, they compromised. The Newberry is a blend of their competing visions.
Aerial photograph of the Newberry, 2022
Architectural detail on the Newberry's facade
A quiet study space on the Newberry's third floor
Over the years, the Newberry has grown and evolved, notably with the addition of a climate-controlled stacks building in the early 1980s and a renovation that updated spaces and restored original architectural details on the library’s first floor in 2018.
You’ll get a healthy dose of history on this tour. But you’ll also get to see the Newberry in action in the present. Tens of thousands of people visit the Newberry every year, and there are many ways that we make the library’s collections, programs, and resources accessible and relevant to them.
This tour is free, and no advance registration is required. We'll meet in the lobby of the Newberry and begin the tour from there.

title: Guangxu Yang (University of Southern California): Exponential Quantum Advantage in Number-on-Forehead Communication [Combinatorics and TCS seminar]
description:
Communication complexity provides a natural setting for demonstrating quantum advantage without computational hardness assumptions. A long line of work has established exponential quantum advantages when two players hold disjoint parts of the input. These results raise a natural question: how does overlap in the players’ input access affect quantum communication advantage?
The number-on-forehead (NOF) model captures a strong form of input overlap: each player sees every input part except their own. This overlap makes classical lower bounds notoriously difficult to prove, and standard techniques such as generalized discrepancy also lower-bound quantum communication.
In this talk, I will focus on an exponential separation between quantum and randomized communication in the one-way NOF model, resolving an open question of Gavinsky and Pudlák (CCC 2008). I will present the main ideas behind the classical lower bound. This part is based on joint work with Jiapeng Zhang. I will conclude by briefly discussing an exponential quantum advantage for a partial Boolean function in the fully interactive NOF model, resolving an open question posed by Göös, Gur, Jain, and Li (STOC 2025). This part is based on joint work with Haoyu Wang and Pei Wu.

title: CEST Workshop: Uma Blanchard
description:
Current Ethnography and Social Theory Workshop on Tuesday, December 1, 4:30-6:00pm
 “Place, Race and History in the Urban Adventure Therapeutic Encounter”
 Presenter: Uma Blanchard, PhD Candidate, Comparative Human Development
 Discussant: Zachary Lazarus, PhD Candidate, Anthropology and Social Work
 Location: Haskell Hall 101
 Abstract: This is a final empirical chapter in my ethnographic dissertation, which follows American adventure therapeutic practice across two different adventure therapy clinics serving teenagers living at opposite ends of the socioeconomic spectrum. Adventure therapy is about metaphorically applying learning and insight from concrete, risky experiences in the wilderness or natural world to one’s emotional life. This chapter hones in on a phenomenon which arises in just one of my field sites: Metro Adventure Therapy, an urban, community-based program serving largely low-income Black and Latino young people living on the south and west sides of Chicago and who live with and amidst significant structural violence. Classically, adventure and wilderness therapy interventions rely on isolation, remoteness and “getting away” as a break from everyday social environments in which to structure a new set of relations and re-build a new type of community. Counter to this model of whisking city kids away to ‘pristine’ places (which critics incisively call the ‘hoods in the woods’ approach), Metro takes care to adventure (mountain biking, paddling, outdoor climbing) primarily close to home—on the south and west sides of Chicago. This chapter will deal with how Metro grounds their practice in unusual spaces, and in doing so, involve meaningful place and rich histories as part of therapeutic process. By running peaceful programs on the south and west sides of Chicago, Metro staff attempt to subvert racialized narratives about ugliness and dejection in the neighborhoods kids hail from. By incorporating narrative about the birth of the environmental justice movement and socially just restoration into programs in places richly steeped in these histories, Metro instills a particular notion about progress, repair, healing and restoration that reflects a concept of human transformation as something beyond individual therapeutic progress.
 For a copy of the pre-circulated paper, please contact the workshop coordinators, Helena Ratté (ratte@uchicago.edu) and/or Hanqi Yang (hanqiy@uchicago.edu).
 Food and refreshments will be available during the workshop. If you have any accommodation needs (e.g., dietary restrictions, accessibility considerations), or any questions, please do not hesitate to reach out to the workshop coordinators.

title: Dipesh Chakrabarty, Christine Laquet, Jennifer Pitts, & Zachary Cahill on the Climate Crisis
description:
Against the backdrop of Nina Chanel Abney’s Threshold exhibition Between Us, Zachary Cahill, Director of Programs and Fellowships at the Gray Center for Arts and Inquiry, moderates a discussion between the 2026-2027 Gray Fellows. Informed by their ongoing collaborative project combining historical inquiry, political theory, and performance, the panelists will discuss how we might move forward in the face of climate change. How do we teach, work, and create when the planet itself faces an unstable future? How do we communicate across generations that will experience the crisis differently? In collaboration with the Gray Center.
 Dipesh Chakrabarty was born in 1948 in Calcutta, India. He holds a bachelor’s degree in Physics from Presidency College, University of Calcutta, a postgraduate degree in Management from the Indian Institute of Management in Calcutta, and a Ph.D. in History from the Australian National University in Canberra. Recognized for his influence in postcolonial studies and criticism of Eurocentrism, Chakrabarty is one of the founders of the Subaltern Studies and Postcolonial Studies editorial boards, as well as a consulting editor for the journal Critical Inquiry and a member of the editorial board of the American Historical Review and Public Culture. He was elected a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 2004, and an honorary fellow of the Australian Academy of the Humanities in 2006. In 2010, he was awarded an honorary doctorate by the University of London, in 2011, by the University of Antwerp, Belgium, and in 2022 by the École Normale Supérieure in Paris. He also received the Distinguished Alumnus award from the Indian Institute of Management in 2011. In 2014, he received the Toynbee Prize in recognition of his contributions to global history. In 2019, he was again awarded the Tagore Memorial Prize, given by the Government of West Bengal, India. Chakrabarty also served as a member of the Council of Experts in Non-Western Art for the Humboldt Forum in Berlin and was part of the Scientific Advisory Board of the Center for Global Cooperation Research in Bonn and Essen from 2012 to 2015. Between 2018 and 2022, he was associated with the Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences at the University of Technology Sydney. In 2023, he was elected a Corresponding Fellow of the British Academy. Additionally, he has been a visiting professor and researcher at institutions such as the Institute for Advanced Study in Berlin, the University of California, Berkeley, Jawaharlal Nehru University in New Delhi, and Princeton University. He has been an honorary professor at the École Normale Supérieure in Paris since 2021 and is the Lawrence A. Kimpton Distinguished Service Professor in the Departments of History and South Asian Languages and Civilizations at the University of Chicago.
 Christine Laquet is a French visual artist whose interdisciplinary practice, informed by ecofeminist perspectives, explores environmental change, speculative thinking, and embodied forms of knowledge. Working across installation, performance, film, photography, and painting, she develops projects through encounters with scientists, research institutions, and more-than-human worlds. Her practice has included scientific expeditions at sea and residencies in research laboratories, engaging subjects ranging from marine ecosystems and microbial life to meteorites, endangered plants, and the return of wolves in collaboration with a naturalist. Her work is structured around three interconnected modes of engagement—BIO, GEO, and EXO—which explore relationships between living organisms, geological matter, and forms of estrangement that open up unfamiliar ways of seeing and relating. Laquet often creates immersive and site-responsive situations where observation, material experimentation, intuition, and speculation intersect. Her work has been exhibited internationally, including at the Musée d’arts de Nantes, FRAC Pays de la Loire, Fondation Louis Vuitton, PyeongChang Biennale, Flux Factory, Pioneer Works, and MAMAM in Recife. Born in Lyon in 1975, she lives and works in Nantes, France.
 Jennifer Pitts is the David and Mary Winton Green Professor in the departments of Political Science and the Committee on Social Thought, and chair of Political Science. She is a political theorist whose research interests lie in the fields of modern political and international thought, particularly the histories of empire and slavery, international law, and debates over global justice. She received her PhD in Government from Harvard University in 2000 and was an assistant professor at Yale and Princeton before coming to the University of Chicago in 2007. She is an editor of the Cambridge University Press series Ideas in Context. At the University of Chicago, she is a fellow of the Chicago Center for Contemporary Theory (3CT), and a member of the faculty boards of the France Chicago Center and the Pozen Family Center for Human Rights. She has recently published articles on eighteenth-century cosmopolitanism and on the antislavery thought of Nicolas de Condorcet, Sophie de Grouchy, and the Afro-British thinker Ottobah Cugoano and continues to work on cosmopolitanism and antislavery in the revolutionary period. She spoke about political theory and planetary history at the Institute for Historical Research in London in November 2025.
 Zachary Cahill is an artist and Director of Programs and Fellowships at the University of Chicago’s Richard and Mary L. Gray Center for Arts and Inquiry, where he also serves at the editor-in-chief of the journal Portable Gray published twice a year by the University of Chicago Press. Cahill has exhibited work in the Smart’s Threshold series and in 2017 co-curated, Revolution Every Day, with the late UChicago Professor Robert Bird and Northwestern University’s Art History Professor Christina Kaier. In 2006, Zachary Cahill received a special commendation for Guard of the Year at the Smart Museum of Art.

title: Joshua Corey, "The Last Words of Jack Ruby" and Robert Archambeau, "The Bloomsbury Forgery"
description:
About The Last Words of Jack Ruby:
Boxers, gangsters, and the JFK assassination: this historical noir novel follows two tough Jews from the streets of Prohibition Chicago to Dealey Plaza and the limits of American myth.
December, 1966. A young FBI agent is summoned by J. Edgar Hoover and sent to Dallas on a secret assignment to interview a dying man who may hold the truth behind one of the most infamous crimes in American history. That man is Jack Ruby—a murderer whose guilt was witnessed live on television, yet whose motives remain shrouded in mystery. Special Agent Bergman finds himself drawn into a web of paranoia and deception in a country unraveling in the wake of the assassination of John F. Kennedy. A disgraced former partner resurfaces, entangled in shadowy Bureau operations. A dancer from Ruby’s past hints at hidden connections. A rogue journalist unfolds conspiracy theories as plausible as they are fantastic. Meanwhile, Ruby— drugged, erratic, and haunted— fixates on his past: Chicago’s underworld, Jewish identity, and his lifelong bond with the boxer, war hero, and drug addict Barney Ross.
Blending historical noir with literary ambition, The Last Words of Jack Ruby explores conspiracy, identity, and the myths that shape a nation. Both gripping thriller and searching meditation, it lingers long after the final page.
About The Bloomsbury Forgery:
When young American painter Ida sails to England during the glittering Jazz Age, she’s chasing both art and passion—specifically, the brilliant poet T.S. Eliot, who might tempt her to leave her husband behind.
In the heady world of Virginia Woolf’s London, Ida brushes shoulders with geniuses and eccentrics before retreating to a grand, possibly haunted country estate to restore a damaged secret portrait of King James and his lover, the Duke of Buckingham. But what begins as an artistic commission soon unravels into a tangle of deceit, forgery, and danger.
As Irish gangsters, English aristocrats, and desperate lovers close in, Ida must rely on her wits—and a ragtag band of artists, heiresses, and dealers—to save a historic home, her family, and perhaps her sanity. Can art, nerve, and a touch of madness be enough to see her through?
About Robert Archambeau:
Robert Archambeau possesses the world’s least interesting international identity. Of French-Canadian ancestry, he was born in Rhode Island, raised in Canada, and spent summers in Maine or at his father’s art studio on a lake in the Canadian wilderness.
His passion for art led to his first novel, Alice B. Toklas is Missing, where the drama of a literary kidnapping takes place amid the artistic tumult of Paris in the 1920s. His ingenue protagonist, Ida Byrne, returns to make her way through gothic chills and literary farce in The Bloomsbury Forgery, where Ida leaves Paris behind for the England of the Virginia Woolf circle.
He lives just outside Chicago with his wife and daughter, who indulge him in his various vices: hanging out in art galleries and museums; collecting paintings and antiques; and owning more tweed and vintage Brooks Brothers clothing than any man should.

title: INTRO TO SCREENWRITING with Alex Lubischer
description:
INTRO TO SCREENWRITING
8 week course
Taught by Alex Lubischer
Tuesdays, Dec 1, 2026 to Feb 2, 2027 from 6:30pm-9:30pm (includes break for the holidays)
$399
Class Description
An introduction to the craft of screenwriting for writers whose background lies in theatre or prose. Throughout the course, we’ll analyze what makes visual storytelling unique while simultaneously interrogating what narrative foundations screenwriting shares with other forms. (The Protagonist, High Stakes, Conflict, etc.) Students are expected to read screenplays of popular films, engage in a rigorous discussion of these scripts, master screenplay formatting, and write a series of short scenes week-to-week. The course culminates with students completing a short film script or beginning the first act of an original feature screenplay.
This class is ideal for theater artists with some background in writing and/or storytelling who want to begin writing films. It's ideal for students interested in learning the difference between writing for the stage and the screen -- as well as what both of these mediums have in common.
About the Instructor
Alex Lubischer is a queer Midwestern writer, born and raised on a farm in Nebraska. He teaches playwriting at DePaul University and Bramble Theatre in Chicago. Current screenwriting projects include BIG DAVE, an hour-long TV pilot co-conceived with Danilo Gambini—Hyperobject Industries is attached to produce—and three features: a 90s-set boy band movie for Division Global and Sappho Screen; an original thriller, EVILDOERS; and a bisexual coming-of-age comedy, THE DEEP END, co-written with Hanna Kime. His latest playwriting project is a new play commission for Raven Theatre. Past plays include PIVOT (Rivendell Theatre Ensemble, Yale School of Drama, GPTC New Play Conference 2024), BOBBIE CLEARLY (Roundabout Theatre Company, Steep Theatre, Jeff Award Winner: Outstanding New Play), YOU DESERVE TO BE HERE (Goodman Playwrights Unit commission; Roundabout Theatre Laura Pels commission, The Bruntwood Prize for Playwriting - Longlist), DO WASPS HAVE DESIRES? (Milwaukee Repertory Theater), WEIRD KIDS (Haven Chicago), THE QUONSETS (Yale Cabaret, co-written with Majkin Holmquist), and SURVEY NO.5 (House of International Theatre, Copenhagen). Lubischer is a former Tow Foundation Playwright-in-Residence at Roundabout Theatre Company. He has developed new work at Playwrights Horizons, Atlantic Theater Company, South Coast Repertory, Page 73, The Orchard Project, SPACE on Ryder Farm, Victory Gardens Theater, First Floor Theater, Red Theatre, The Understudy, and Actors Theatre of Louisville. He has been a semifinalist for the P73 Playwriting Fellowship and a three-time finalist for the O’Neill National Playwrights Conference. MFA: Yale. BA: University of Southern California.

title: Frank Zappa’S America
description:
Tuesday, December 1
Lagunitas Presents
A Gman Author Series Event
Frank Zappas America
Author Bradley Morgan in Conversation with Jill Hopkins
Free with RSVP / 21 & over / Doors: 7pm / Show: 7:30pm
Books available for purchase and signing immediately following
From his early albums with the Mothers of Invention, Frank Zappa established a reputation as a musical genius who pushed the limits of culture throughout the 1960s and 1970s, experimenting with a blend of genres in innovative and unheard-of ways. Not only did his exploratory styles challenge the expectations of what popular music could sound like, but his prolific creative endeavors also shaped how audiences thought about the freedom of artistic expression.
In Frank Zappas America, Bradley Morgan casts the artist as an often-misunderstood figure who critiqued the actions of religious and political groups promoting a predominantly white, Christian vision of the United States. A controversial and provocative satirist, often criticized for the shocking subject matter of his songs, Zappa provided social commentary throughout his career that spoke truth to power about the nefarious institutions operating in the lives of everyday Americans. Beginning in the late 1970s, his music frequently addressed the rise of extremist religious influence in American politics, specifically white Christian nationalism.
Join Bradley and Jill Hopkins in a conversation about the book, the man, his music, and his ideas about the country, and how many of them are still applicable today.

title: Tituba
description:
To better understand the real Titubas plight, I read the tran­scripts of the 1692 trials. As Tituba comes to life, speaking in real time, her confession is every bit as enthralling and suspenseful as any of the most dramatic scenes in Millers play. -Winsome Pinnock, The Yale Review
Performed in the hallowed halls of the University of Chicagos historic Rockefeller Memorial Chapel, the 2026/27 season opens with the American premiere of Titubaa theatrical experience that offers a new lens on pre-Revolutionary War America through spiritually charged language, music, and dance.
In this solo performance, Titubathe real-life person accused in the Salem witch trials of 1692 and featured in Arthur Millers classic, The Crucibleinvites the audience to journey through her mystical, sonically complex world to hear her side of the story. With care and wry humor, she details her history with the girls in Salem Village, her beloved mother and husband, Reverend Parriss rage, the violence of enslavement, and her unspoken indigenous name, building to a scathing climax and the ignition of historic mass hysteria.
Set against the backdrop of the institution that accused Tituba centuries ago, Associate Artistic Director Gabrielle Randle-Bent directs, with dramaturgy by Marilyn F. Vitale Artistic Director Avery Willis Hoffman. Together, they bring Titubas life story to light in a sacred place, uplifting her voice and showcasing the transformational power of storytelling.
All performances will be held at the University of Chicagos Rockefeller Chapel, located at 5850 S Woodlawn Ave, Chicago.
Dates for Tituba will be announced in summer 2026. Seating at Rockefeller Memorial Chapel is general admission, but subscribers receive access to the preferred section.
Subscriptions including this production are on sale now and can be purchased online or by calling (773) 753-4472. Individual tickets will go on sale September 1st.

address: 111 E. Wacker Dr., Suite 1321, Chicago, IL, 60601
description:
Join Elias Kalach, architect, co-founder and creative director of Vertebral, as he explores the design philosophy and creative process behind a decade of work.
Completed in 2021, Casa Escalera stands inside a forest near Valle de Bravo, Mexico, adapting to the natural topography of the site. Photo by Camila Sh.
Vertebral is an architecture studio known for its thoughtful use of materials and designs that respond to their surroundings. The firm approaches architecture as a way to highlight a site's existing character, incorporating elements such as reclaimed timber, existing structures and native landscapes into its projects. Primarily focused on residential work, the studio’s completed and ongoing projects span a range of settings, from urban neighborhoods to coastal, rainforest and desert environments.
Following the lecture, architect, curator and educator Iker Gil, founder of MAS Studio and the nonprofit MAS Context, joins Elias for a conversation about the role of art in architecture, Vertebral’s approach to contributing to Mexico’s modernist and contemporary design legacy and how architects can build partnerships beyond their clients to support design excellence.
Prior to the lecture, attendees are invited to a 5 p.m. reception outside the CAC Lecture Hall with light bites and refreshments.

With an unwavering belief in the baritone saxophone’s storytelling power, Farace has earned praise from some of jazz’s most respected voices. DownBeat Magazine hailed him as “an outstanding new voice on baritone saxophone,” while saxophone legend Gary Smulyan noted: “His baritone playing is deeply emotional, mature, and his sound simply gorgeous. The combination of the writing and playing is stunning, wonderfully conceived, and in perfect balance and harmony.” 
For A Swinging Christmas, the Jimmy Farace Quartet joins forces with acclaimed Chicago vocalist Anna Donnelly for an evening of classic Christmas favorites infused with the warmth, swing, and spirit of jazz. title: Christmas with the Abram Collier Nonet
address: 10 S. Vail Ave., Arlington Heights, IL, 60005
description:
The Abram Collier Nonet returns to Hey Nonny to celebrate the release of their new album, 'Christmas With The Abram Collier Nonet'. Ring in the holiday season with a special evening full of new takes on beloved Christmas tunes and other holiday classics played straight off of the record!
Vocalist and baritone saxophonist Abram Collier brings together a band of eight of Chicago's finest jazz musicians to form the Abram Collier Nonet. The group performs a variety of original, ensemble-exclusive arrangements, ranging from jazz standards and repertoire from the Great American Songbook, to selections from modern pop music and video game soundtracks adapted for jazz ensemble. title: 2nd Set With Chi-Town Trumpet Summit
description:
A collaboration between Andy’s Jazz Club and Marques Carroll, The Trumpet Summit features the most in demand and on the rise trumpeters in the city of Chicago. Showcased in the group are three trumpets of rotating pairs joining leader Marques Carroll on stage. The band will be celebrating the music of the greats like Freddie Hubbard, Wynton Marsalis, Lee Morgan as well as original music from each individual Summit trumpeters.
For the diverse trumpeter who has spent the last 28 years of life pursuing music with dedication and determination, Marques Carroll has turned his passion into a career and a life long journey. To say that Jazz is his only plateau would limit his overall playing ability and knowledge of music. From what his father, graphic design artist and novice funk bassist, Mark Carroll, would say, “He would listen to everything, even when he was about 5 years old, but Jazz music is what caught his attention.”
During his time in Chicago, Marques became a first call sub for the Chicago Jazz Ensemble while under the direction of Dana Hall where he would play section or lead trumpet for the ensemble and perform with artists such as Christian McBride, Etienne Charles, Meshell Ndegocello and Nicholas Payton.
Marques continues to stay active in music education throughout the city of Chicago. Currently the Musical Director for the Chicago Jesuit Academy, Marques has written the course outline and curriculum in which students are exposed to jazz history, theory and instrumental pedagogy.

Raised in a small beach town outside of Tampa, Florida, Dave Herrero was introduced to the local and national music scene though a family friend, sneaking out of military school at age 15 to regularly to see bands like the Arc Angels and Johnny Winter, and to go to a local blues jam at the Green Iguana on Monday nights, where local heroes like James and Lucky Peterson would frequently pop in.
Herrero got his start as a professional touring musician in 1996 in Jacksonville Beach, Florida, then moved to Austin, TX and joined Archie Bell and the Drells (of "Tighten Up" fame). In Austin, he quickly immersed himself into the Austin music community, playing with the likes of Gary Clark Jr, Charlie Sexton, Lazy Lester, Matt Powell, Seth Walker all the while starting the Blues Society of Austin with friends, Mark "Kaz" Kazanoff, Nancy Coplin and Nicole Shiro. It was in Austin that Dave honed in on his guitar playing, singing and songwriting skills, that he then took with him to Chicago. More about Dave Herrero

title: Created Equal: The Premises and Promises of the Declaration of Independence
location: Regenstein Library, The Special Collections Research Center
description:
On July 2, 1776, the Continental Congress voted to declare independence from Great Britain. Two days later, delegates in Philadelphia finalized a document designed to announce and explain that act to readers in America and Europe.
 The Declaration of Independence asserted the revolutionary right of a people to alter or abolish a government, grounding that principle in the “self-evident” claims that “all Men are created Equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights” and “that among these are Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness.”
 Over time, many readers have come to consider the radical philosophical premises in the Declaration as founding political promises of the United States. In doing so, they transformed an indictment of the British King and a manifesto of secession from the British Empire into an American charter of liberty, equality, and rights.
 But the Declaration’s meaning has never been solitary. From the start, readers disagreed about what its authors intended. Since 1776, radically different interpretations of the Declaration’s ideas have been put to different ends—from demands for the legal, political, and social equality of all persons, to claims for the rights of states to secede from the union, to calls for the revolutionary overthrow of the government.
 How did the Declaration’s premises become its promises? Drawing on rare materials from the seventeenth century to the present, this exhibition invites you to explore the document’s meanings in its own time, to consider contested interpretations across history, and to reflect on what the Declaration means today.
 Curator
 Eric Slauter, Associate Professor, Department of English Language and Literature; Associate faculty member, Divinity School; Founding Director of the Karla Scherer Center for the Study of American Culture; The University of Chicago

Visitors to the University of Chicago Library may obtain an entry pass by checking in at Regenstein Library’s entry desk and presenting a current, government-issued photo ID, such as a driver’s license, CityKey, state ID, or passport to confirm identity. Get more visitor information.

title: Sewn as One
description:
Sewn as One is a textile installation by the Science, Art, and Sustainability (SAS) team of the Phoenix Sustainability Initiative (PSI), in partnership with Creative Chicago Reuse Exchange (CCRx). On view in the 2nd Floor South Cantilever Lounge at the Logan Center for the Arts.
 The Phoenix Sustainability Initiative (PSI) is a student-led organization at the University of Chicago dedicated to promoting environmental awareness and integrating sustainable practices throughout campus and surrounding communities. Through collaborative partnerships, inclusive community-building, and creative approaches to environmental challenges, PSI encourages students to develop the skills and collective agency necessary to enact tangible change. Its Science, Art, and Sustainability
 (SAS) project group brings these commitments into artistic practice, exploring how material reuse, collective making, and creative experimentation can cultivate environmental responsibility and meaningful connections.
 Collaborating with Creative Chicago Reuse Exchange, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that redistributes donated surplus materials for artists, hobbyists, and educators, the SAS project group transforms upcycled fabrics into a tapestry of collective care and environmental awareness. Through a series of open, hands-on mending workshops, the project invites participants to reconsider mark-making not only as gaining technical skill, but as a social and ecological practice.
 Over the course of two academic quarters, three-hour “Sewing Sunday” sessions were held by SAS and open to anyone on campus or passing through the work space, encouraging both experienced makers and first-time participants to sew, patch, embroider, and mend donated textiles. Each contribution—a series of stitching, patchwork, or conversation—becomes part of the evolving textured surface of the work.
 The accumulated labor, dialogue, experimentation, and learning from these sessions culminated into the large-scale fabric installation that spans the hallway of Logan Center for the Arts’ South Cantilever Lounge. The final tapestries act as visual records of foregrounding sustainability, slow making, and community engagement while tracing how individual acts of care can coalesce into an exuberant, communicative form.

title: Time, Fragmented
description:
Time, Fragmented asks what it means for a place to be shaped by complex social and environmental histories, and how distinct but interrelated histories coalesce to create a collective narrative. Along these lines, the exhibition considers contemporary practices of unearthing, both literally and figuratively, and investigates remnants of times past, piecing together the story that unfolds thereafter. In the context of shifting regional powers and migrating stories, Time, Fragmented illuminates the (hi)stories foundational to modern-day Turkey, tracing diasporas of culture, thought, and practice.
 Materials entail historic postcards and photographs from the turn of the twentieth century displayed from a family collection by İbrahim Selim Ergöz. Additionally, building and ornamental materials from the Joel Snyder Materials Collection are displayed alongside photographs and maps from historic expeditions from the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures Archives. Finally, multi-media works from New Orleans-based Turkish artist, Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes are presented alongside personal ephemera from the artist and curator. Through a variety of items from polyphonic sources, Time, Fragmented engages with the many layers of history—witnessed through a mosaic of lived reality, filtered through glimpses of past experiences—that live in time.
 Curator
 Time, Fragmented is curated by Defne Ergöz, BA/MA ’27, an Environment, Geography, and Urbanization major and Architectural Studies minor in the College, concurrently pursuing an MA in Art History.
 Artists
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes (Turkish, b. 1997)
 Deniz Türkoğlu Hewes lives and works in New Orleans, Louisiana since 2024. Türkoğlu Hewes is a conceptual photographer, building worlds for a single frame that carry the immaterial nature of emotions to a physical realm, portraying their silent dictate on lived experiences. The artist focuses on conflicting collective and personal agendas, evaluating dynamics between discipline and intuition, culture and callings. Her Turkish identity and upbringing rooted in strong familial ties appears in her recent work completed in İstanbul. The coexistence of culture and nature in her work criticizes the misconception of full control over emotional environments, similar to the power assumed over natural ecosystems. Türkoğlu Hewes studied fine arts, film and theater at Northwestern University. Her work has been exhibited in the 2025 Louisiana Contemporary at the Ogden Museum of Southern Art. She has been included in exhibitions at Soho Photo Gallery in New York City, Barın Han in İstanbul, and the Contemporary Art Center in New Orleans.
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz (Turkish, b. 1971)
 İbrahim Selim Ergöz, the curator’s father, currently resides in Westchester, New York. Ergöz has been collecting antique ephemera since he was fifteen, with a vast collection spanning his interests in historical documentation and postal items, especially as it concerns the Middle East North Africa region. His archive ranges from widely-available materials to rare collectibles. Time, Fragmented is the first instance Ergöz’s collection will be on public display.
 Support
 CWAC Exhibitions is organized by the Department of Art History’sVisual Resources Center. Additional support for the exhibition is provided by the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, the Committee on Environment, Geography, and Urbanization, the Master of Arts Program in the Humanities, and Architectural Studies.
 The CWAC Exhibitions team includes Katie Chen, Scarlet Ding, Jiayi Laura Feng, Natalie Hsu, Grace Newby, Kseniya Portnaya, Stephanie Strother, and Yanlin Zhu.
